issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'Similar cars' is hard to reconcile as a salient trigger unless there is a very specific undisclosed trauma context; it reads as a transport/accident-associated cue rather than illness-related.

'Related people/known people' can occur around illness trauma, but paired with other selected triggers and threat items it suggests an interpersonal or assault-like threat context more than a medical illness context.

Scanning for exits is much more characteristic of fear of external attack or entrapment than of trauma centered on life-threatening illness, and is difficult to connect coherently to the rest of an illness-based profile.
Reacting to unexpected nearby movement as if in danger is also more typical of assault/combat-type threat expectations than illness trauma, creating a mismatch with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'Being Praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless paired with illness-specific meanings elsewhere (e.g., praise for surviving, coping, or returning to function). No corresponding appraisal or memory content makes this trigger clinically coherent here.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The threat items 'Scanning Exits' and 'Startle to Movement' imply a danger formulation centered on assault/attack or external interpersonal threat, which is difficult to reconcile with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you' similarly reflects fear of intentional human harm rather than recurrence of illness, bodily catastrophe, medical procedures, or death from disease. This is poorly aligned with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Going Out' would be coherent if linked to infection fears, collapse in public, or medical reminders, but those meanings are not represented in the trigger, threat, or appraisal items selected. As written, it appears to address a different threat context than the rest of the profile.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'related people' as a trigger is plausible, but the profile otherwise anchors triggers strongly in medical reminders and bodily danger rather than interpersonal threat. This item becomes hard to reconcile because the accompanying appraisal and threat items do not explain why known people specifically function as a major trigger.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'You can never know who will harm you' implies an interpersonal perpetrator-based worldview. That is difficult to align with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness, especially when the rest of the profile centers medical cues, sleep disturbance, startle, and physical reactivity rather than harm from other people. A more illness- or vulnerability-focused appraisal would fit better.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, medical triggers like needles, drips, and procedures are coherent, but alcohol smell is not plausibly linked to the trauma context unless there is additional undisclosed treatment context; it stands out as a hard-to-explain trigger relative to the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a 19-year-old male with life-threatening illness trauma. The other appraisals center on bodily vulnerability and loss of meaning, whereas a failed core-role appraisal implies a specific disrupted identity or responsibility that is otherwise absent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out
issues.explanation: Avoiding going out is weakly connected to the rest of the selected items. The profile is dominated by medical reminders and internal threat/bodily vulnerability, so broad avoidance of leaving home lacks a clear clinical target here and is not well explained by the trigger-threat-appraisal pattern shown.

vignette:
Callum is a nineteen-year-old of Scottish descent who works as a residential counselor at a youth camp outside Portland. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 67 following a life-threatening illness diagnosed fourteen months ago - a rapid-onset bacterial infection that progressed to septic shock within forty-eight hours of his first symptoms. He spent eleven days in the intensive care unit, during which he was intubated, subjected to multiple central-line insertions, and kept sedated for much of the admission. The smell of the ward - that flat, chemical antiseptic odor - saturated everything: his skin, the pillowcases his mother brought from home, the air he breathed through the ventilator mask before sedation took hold. The needles came without warning, the drips multiplied, and his body, which had always felt reliable and young, became something that was failing him in real time and in public.

Callum was discharged physically recovered but psychologically altered in ways that neither he nor his family initially had language for. The first sign that something was wrong came when a routine blood draw for a follow-up appointment sent him into a full panic response - heart hammering, vision narrowing, the absolute bodily conviction that he was back in the ICU. Medical equipment such as needles or drips, the sight of an ambulance on the street, the antiseptic smell that clings to any hospital corridor - each of these became reliable detonators. When triggered, Callum's body floods with physical reactivity: his heart rate spikes, his hands shake, and he experiences the kind of full-system alarm that feels indistinguishable from the original emergency. Unexpected movement nearby - a colleague crossing behind him quickly, a camper running past - produces a startle response so sharp it embarrasses him. Sleep has become fractured and unreliable, and he lies awake most nights unable to locate the border between waking vigilance and the edge of rest.

What has frightened Callum most, and what he returns to again and again in early sessions, is not the memory of the illness itself but what it revealed: that his body cannot be trusted. He had come to believe, with quiet and total conviction, that his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is safe - that it is working against him rather than for him. This sense of the body as enemy has deepened into something broader. Nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore; the things that once anchored him - his relationships, his work with young people, the plans he had made - seem to float at a distance he cannot close. These appraisals do not stay still. They reach back into the trigger landscape: because he believes his body is fundamentally unreliable, ordinary physical sensations become evidence of renewed threat, and the threshold at which a stimulus registers as dangerous has dropped dramatically.

The maintaining cycles have accumulated quietly over months. Because triggers produce such overwhelming physical reactivity, Callum began structuring his life around avoidance - rerouting his drives to bypass the hospital district, declining a physical examination his GP recommended, leaving a training session at work when a first-aid demonstration brought out a kit containing a needle. The avoidance of medical cues has become so entrenched that he recently missed a mandatory health screening required by his employer, which has placed his counselor position under review - a concrete consequence that finally alarmed him enough to seek help. His threat state, meanwhile, feeds directly back into avoidance: the hyperarousal and poor sleep leave him depleted and raw, which lowers his tolerance for any reminder and makes withdrawal feel not like a choice but like survival. He stays up until very late each night, partly because lying in the dark with nothing to do amplifies the bodily sensations he dreads, and this chronic sleep deprivation sharpens his startle responses and physical reactivity the following day, tightening the loop further. He has also begun avoiding anything discussed in therapy - a new and worrying development - retreating from the material almost as soon as a session ends, which has slowed progress and left him more isolated inside the experience.

Callum came to his first appointment accompanied by his partner, who has noticed the withdrawal and the sleeplessness and who, he said quietly, deserves better than this. What he most fears is that the body he cannot trust will humiliate him again. What he most hopes is that something in him might still be reachable.
